claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation in nanoscale FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings under sustained loading is governed by interface-mediated dislocation climb.
Severe lattice distortion and short-range order slow atomic diffusion along FCC/BCC interfaces.
Interface density is the dominant control on creep rate in the proposed multilayers.
The initial coating consists of alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers, each 10 nm thick.
The HEA layers are random solid solutions exhibiting severe lattice distortion and measurable short-range order.
Changing individual layer thickness among 5 nm, 10 nm, and 20 nm at constant total coating thickness changes the density of FCC/BCC interfaces.
The controlled comparison maintains identical alloy compositions and deposition conditions across layer-thickness variants.
During sustained loading, dislocations glide into FCC/BCC interfaces.
Dislocations at the interfaces must climb to accommodate continued deformation.
Dislocation climb in these multilayers is diffusion-limited.
Higher interface density produced by thinner layers slows dislocation climb and therefore lowers the creep rate.
The 10 nm baseline has a steady-state creep rate of approximately 1×10^-6 s^-1 under the specified test conditions.
The 5 nm multilayer will have a steady-state creep rate of approximately 5×10^-7 s^-1, about half the 10 nm baseline rate.
The 20 nm multilayer will have a steady-state creep rate of approximately 2×10^-6 s^-1, about twice the 10 nm baseline rate.
The proposed relationship is valid only for layer thicknesses of 5–20 nm, temperatures of 0.5–0.6 Tm, and stresses below 150 MPa.
The proposed relationship requires random-solid-solution HEA layers that undergo no phase transformations during creep.
The scaling exponent relating interface spacing to creep rate and the quantitative effect of short-range order on diffusion coefficients are uncertain.
A failure of creep rate to decrease with increasing interface density, including the 5 nm sample creeping as fast as or faster than the 20 nm sample, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The phrase 'creep rate will decrease approximately inversely with interface spacing' is mathematically inconsistent with both the numerical predictions and the mechanism. The predicted rates imply creep rate increases with interface spacing and decreases with interface density.
